expectations.description: Explains Rasch as equal-discrimination across items, while 2PL allows discriminations to vary
expectations.note: Clearly explained with the mathematical formulas and description: 'Rasch constrains all discriminations to be equal... 2PL says: items differ in how well they differentiate ability, and we should model that.'

expectations.description: Frames the Rasch vs. 2PL choice as a substantive measurement-philosophy decision, not just an AIC/BIC comparison
expectations.note: Explicitly stated in opening and dedicated section: 'This is why you shouldn't choose based on AIC/BIC alone.' Discusses Andrich/Wright tradition vs Birnbaum/Lord tradition as philosophical stances.

expectations.description: Mentions specific objectivity or sample-independence as a property of the Rasch model
expectations.note: Dedicated section on specific objectivity with both definitions: item parameters independent of person sample, person parameters independent of item sample. Linked to practical applications (test banking, equating, CAT).

expectations.description: States that N = 800 is adequate for 2PL (or for either model)
expectations.note: Explicitly states: 'Your sample size is solidly adequate. Rasch needs roughly 250+ for stable estimation; 2PL needs ~500. At N = 800 with 30 items, both models will give you stable, reliable parameter estimates.'

expectations.description: Provides mirt R code example (mirt::mirt with itemtype='Rasch' and/or '2PL')
expectations.note: Full R code block includes both mirt(data, 1, itemtype='2PL') and mirt(data, 1, itemtype='Rasch') with coef(), anova(), itemfit(), M2(), plot(), and fscores() examples.

expectations.description: Mentions item information function (IIF) or test information function (TIF)
expectations.note: Both IIF and TIF mentioned with explanation of what they represent, code to plot them, and practical guidance on using TIF for cut-score decision-making.

expectations.description: Does not recommend 3PL as a default for a knowledge test without considering whether guessing is substantively relevant
expectations.note: 3PL section explicitly cautions against it: 'I'd be cautious about 3PL... The question to ask is substantive: is guessing meaningfully happening in your test context? Not: does 3PL fit better by AIC?'
